segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan and was being led by the Spirit in the wilderness

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for forty days, being tested by the devil. He ate nothing during those days, and when they were over he was hungry.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The devil said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “If you are the Son of God, tell this stone to become bread.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus answered him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “It is written: ‘A person will not live on bread alone.’”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then, leading him up, he showed him all the kingdoms of the inhabited world in an instant of time,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and the devil said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “To you I will give all this authority and their glory, for it has been handed over to me, and I give it to whomever I wish.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: So if you will bow in worship before me, it will all be yours.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus answered him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “It is written: ‘You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve.’”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then the devil brought him to Jerusalem, set him on the highest point of the temple, and said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down from here,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: for it is written: ‘He will command his angels concerning you, to guard you,’

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: and: ‘On their hands they will lift you up, so that you do not strike your foot against a stone.’”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus answered him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “It has been said: ‘You shall not put the Lord your God to the test.’”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When the devil had finished every test, he withdrew from him until an opportune time.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then Jesus returned to Galilee in the power of the Spirit, and news about him went out through the whole surrounding region.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He was teaching in their synagogues and was praised by everyone.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He came to Nazareth, where he had been brought up, and as was his custom he went into the synagogue on the Sabbath day and stood up to read.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The scroll of the prophet Isaiah was handed to him, and unrolling the scroll he found the place where it was written:

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me to bring good news to the poor. He has sent me to proclaim release to captives and recovery of sight to the blind, to send the oppressed out in release,

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: to proclaim the year of the Lord’s favor.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then he rolled up the scroll, gave it back to the attendant, and sat down. The eyes of everyone in the synagogue were fixed on him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he began to say to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Today this scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: All spoke well of him and marveled at the words of grace that came from his mouth, and they were saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Isn’t this Joseph’s son?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “No doubt you will quote me this proverb: ‘Physician, heal yourself! What we have heard happened in Capernaum, do here in your hometown as well.’”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Truly I tell you, no prophet finds favor in his hometown.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But in truth I tell you, there were many widows in Israel in the days of Elijah, when the sky was shut for three years and six months and a great famine came over all the land,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: yet Elijah was sent to none of them, but only to Zarephath in the territory of Sidon, to a widow there.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And there were many people with skin disease in Israel in the time of the prophet Elisha, yet none of them was cleansed, but only Naaman the Syrian.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Everyone in the synagogue was filled with rage on hearing this.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They got up, drove him out of the town, and led him to the brow of the hill on which their town was built, intending to throw him off the cliff.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But he passed through the middle of them and went on his way.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He went down to Capernaum, a town in Galilee, and was teaching them on the Sabbath.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They were astounded at his teaching, because his word had authority.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: In the synagogue there was a man who had the spirit of an unclean demon, and he cried out with a loud voice,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Ha! What have you to do with us, Jesus of Nazareth? Have you come to destroy us? I know who you are: the Holy One of God.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus rebuked him, saying,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Be silent, and come out of him!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then the demon threw the man down in their midst and came out of him without doing him any harm.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Amazement came over them all, and they kept saying to one another,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “What is this word? For with authority and power he commands the unclean spirits, and they come out!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And talk of him was spreading to every place in the surrounding region.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He got up and left the synagogue and went into Simon’s house. Simon’s mother-in-law was suffering from a high fever, and they appealed to him on her behalf.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Standing over her, he rebuked the fever, and it left her. At once she got up and began to serve them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: As the sun was setting, all who had people sick with various diseases brought them to him, and laying his hands on each one of them, he healed them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Demons also came out of many, shouting,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “You are the Son of God!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But he rebuked them and would not allow them to speak, because they knew that he was the Messiah.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When day came, he went out and made his way to a deserted place. The crowds were searching for him, and they came to where he was and tried to keep him from leaving them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But he said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “I must bring the good news of the kingdom of God to the other towns as well, because that is what I was sent for.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he went on proclaiming in the synagogues of Judea.

notes.note: The Greek verb covers both testing and tempting, and most translations have 'tempted' here. 'Tested' is used because the scene echoes Israel's forty years of testing in the wilderness, and Jesus answers each time from that part of Deuteronomy. It also keeps the link with verse 12, where a compound of the same verb means putting God to the test, and with the related noun in verse 13. The devil's aim is certainly to make Jesus fail, so 'tempted' is not wrong.

Luke does not use the general word for 'world' here but a term meaning the inhabited earth, which in his day often meant in practice the Roman empire and its neighbours. Most translations simply have 'the world'. The parallel in Matthew uses the more general word.

notes.phrase: the highest point of the temple
notes.note: The Greek word means a tip, edge or projecting part (literally 'little wing'), and it is not known which feature of the temple complex is meant. Suggestions include the roof edge of the sanctuary and a corner of the outer colonnades overlooking the Kidron valley. The traditional 'pinnacle' suggests a spire, which the temple did not have.

notes.phrase: to bring good news to the poor
notes.traditional: to preach the gospel to the poor; he hath sent me to heal the brokenhearted
notes.note: Many later manuscripts add 'to heal the brokenhearted' after 'he has sent me', which brings the quotation into line with Isaiah 61:1. The earliest witnesses lack the phrase, and it is generally regarded as a scribal addition. The quotation as Luke gives it combines Isaiah 61:1–2 with a line from Isaiah 58:6.

The same Greek noun appears twice in this verse and is rendered 'release' both times. It is the word Luke regularly uses for the forgiveness of sins. In the Greek Old Testament it is also the term for the release of debts and slaves in the Jubilee year. A first-century hearer could catch both associations, which English cannot convey with one word.

The phrase can mean that Jesus spoke winningly ('gracious words') or that he spoke about God's grace. Most translations choose the first, and the rendering here leaves both open. The crowd's reaction is also debated. Most take it as admiration that sours as Jesus goes on, but a minority reads the verbs as hostile from the start ('testified against him').

The Greek adjective here is the same one used in verse 19 for the year 'of the Lord’s favor' (traditionally 'the acceptable year of the Lord'). It is rendered with 'favor' in both places so that the echo is audible. Jesus proclaims the year of God's favor and finds none in his own town.
The Greek word means both 'heaven' and 'sky'. Here it refers to the visible sky as the source of rain, and 'the sky was shut' is an idiom for drought. The story is told in 1 Kings 17–18.

notes.phrase: Zarephath in the territory of Sidon
notes.note: Zarephath was a Phoenician town outside Israel, and Naaman in the next verse was a commander in the army of Syria, Israel's enemy (1 Kings 17; 2 Kings 5). Both of Jesus' examples are foreigners who received what Israelites did not. That explains the fury of the synagogue in verse 28.

The traditional 'lepers' suggests modern leprosy (Hansen's disease). The Greek term, following the Hebrew of Leviticus 13–14, covered a range of skin conditions that made a person ritually unclean, which is why the cure is called being 'cleansed'. It is widely agreed that the biblical term is broader than the modern disease, though many translations keep 'lepers' for familiarity.

The Greek word may be an exclamation of surprise or displeasure, or the imperative of a verb meaning 'let be', which gives the older rendering 'Let us alone!'. Most recent scholarship takes it as an exclamation. The question that follows is an idiom, literally 'What to us and to you?', meaning roughly 'Why are you interfering with us?'

The Greek word, traditionally 'Christ', is here a title with the article: the anointed king Israel was expecting. 'Messiah' is used where the title itself is the point, and 'Christ' where the word functions as a name. Several modern translations make the same distinction.

The earliest manuscripts read 'Judea', while many later ones read 'Galilee', which fits the surrounding narrative and the parallel in Mark 1:39. 'Judea' is the harder reading and is probably original, with 'Galilee' a scribal correction. Luke sometimes uses 'Judea' broadly for the whole land of the Jews, Galilee included, and that is likely the sense here.

candidates.reason: The verb and its noun πειρασμός recur across the Gospels, letters and the Lord's Prayer, and translators split between 'tempt/temptation' and 'test/trial'; the choice needs to be made once.
It is usually 'forgiveness' (of sins) but 'release' in Jubilee contexts like this one, so the relationship between the two renderings should be settled for the whole New Testament.
'Leper/leprosy' misleads modern readers toward Hansen's disease; the word recurs through the Synoptics and needs one consistent rendering.
It ranges from physical prostration before a superior to worship of God, and translators vary between 'worship', 'bow down' and 'pay homage' in ways that affect christological passages.
It is distinct from κόσμος and sometimes means in effect the Roman empire (Luke 2:1; Acts), so a decision is needed on whether to mark the difference in English.
